title: When a property manager refuses to make repairs: tracking requests on Mac
metaTitle: Property manager refuses to make repairs: tracking requests on Mac
description: If your property manager refuses to make repairs, you need a clear paper trail. Learn to track maintenance requests on your Mac effectively.
targetKeyword: property manager refuses to make repairs
intro: When a property manager refuses to make repairs, the first step is building a bulletproof record of every request. You must document every communication to protect your rights as a tenant or owner. On your Mac, you can centralize these records using simple tools like Mail, Notes, and Sheets. This guide shows you how to organize your documentation to force action.
tldr: Centralize all maintenance requests in one digital folder.
Use time-stamped emails instead of phone calls for every repair request.
Keep a log of all correspondence, including dates, photos, and follow-ups.
Understand your local tenant rights regarding habitability and repairs.
Use your Mac to keep these records organized and easily accessible.

blocks.text: When a property manager refuses to make repairs, they often rely on the lack of a formal record. If you only call them on the phone, there is no proof of your request. You need a written trail. This trail serves as your primary evidence if you need to escalate the issue. Start by creating a dedicated folder in your Mail app on your Mac. Name it Repair Requests. Move every email regarding a specific repair into this folder. If you have physical receipts or paper documents, use the Preview app to scan them into PDFs. Press ⌘ + N in Preview to create a new document from your scanner. Keep your files named clearly with dates, such as 2026-11-13-Repair-Request-Kitchen-Sink. This simple naming convention helps you find documents quickly in Spotlight.

Inefficient request tracking creates massive friction. When maintenance requests are scattered across texts, emails, and calls, things get lost. For a property manager, this chaos leads to burnout. For a tenant, it leads to ignored repairs. If you are a manager, you lose money on every manual entry. If you are a tenant, you lose the comfort of a functional home. The cost of a manager leaving due to this burnout is between $45,000 and $60,000. This includes recruiting and training new staff. When you track your own requests, you are not just helping yourself. You are making the entire system work better for everyone involved.
How to document your repair requests

items: Send every request in writing via email. Do not rely on verbal agreements.
Take clear photos or videos of the issue. Store these in a dated folder on your Mac.
Use a spreadsheet to track the date of the request, the date of acknowledgment, and the current status.
Include specific details like the exact location, the nature of the problem, and the impact on your living situation.
Keep copies of all replies from the property manager, even if they are dismissive.

blocks.text: Using your Mac to stay organized

Your Mac has built-in tools that make this easier. Use the Notes app to keep a running log of your interactions. Press ⌘ + Control + Space to open the emoji picker if you need to flag important notes. Use Apple Reminders to set follow-up tasks. If you haven't heard back in three days, set a reminder to send a follow-up email. You can even use the Universal Clipboard to copy text from your iPhone and paste it directly into a document on your Mac. This is useful if you take photos of a repair issue with your phone and need to attach them to an email on your computer.

If you have a clear, documented history of requests and the property manager still refuses to make repairs, you may need to escalate. Check your local housing laws. Many jurisdictions have specific procedures for tenants when a landlord fails to maintain a property. You might need to send a formal letter via certified mail. Keep a digital copy of this letter on your Mac. You can use the Pages app to draft this letter. Ensure you cite the specific dates and details you have been tracking in your spreadsheet. Having this data ready makes the process much faster.

faq.question: What should I do if my property manager ignores my emails?
faq.answer: If they ignore your emails, continue to send follow-ups and keep a record of every attempt. After a reasonable period, consider sending a formal letter via certified mail and consult your local tenant rights resources.

faq.question: How do I organize my repair documents on a Mac?
faq.answer: Create a dedicated folder in your Mail app for requests. Use the Notes app to keep a log of dates and interactions. Store photos in a dated folder on your Mac's hard drive.

faq.question: Is it legal to record phone calls with my property manager?
faq.answer: Recording laws vary by state and country. Always check your local laws before recording any conversation. Written communication is generally safer and easier to track.
